newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Robotics to offer cable modem and system.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Robotics to offer cable modem and system.

text.p: U.S. Robotics Corp., the No. 1 maker of consumer computer modems, said Monday it is introducing a system for providing super-fast Internet access over cable television networks.
U.S. Robotics, which late last month agreed to be acquired by network equipment company 3Com Corp. in a $7.3 billion stock deal, also said it is working with cable operators to develop the market.
The Skokie, Ill.-based company said its system gives cable TV operators a new way to deliver data over cable quickly and cost-effectively.

The new system is designed for rapid distribution, as well as long-term flexibility for cable operators, U.S. Robotics said in a statement. Cable TV operators will be able to use the product while completing the costly process of converting their cable networks to two-way systems.

Industry analysts said the cable modem is the next logical step for U.S. Robotics, whose modems using conventional telephone lines are on more desktops around the world than any other company's. Modems enable computers to communicate over phone lines and through other means such as cable.
"The U.S. Robotics' move is good for the company because it is an extension of its analog modem business," said Amar Senan, an analyst with investment bankers Volpe, Welty & Co.

Connection to the Internet or to other networks is much faster over cable than over phone lines. Phone-line access can be so slow that some users jokingly refer to the World Wide Web as the "World Wide Wait."
U.S. Robotics said it created a cable access business unit and will demonstrate the new system March 17-19 at the National Cable Television Association Cable 97 trade show in New Orleans.

U.S. Robotics said the cable access business unit is in talks with cable operators and expects to begin technical and field trials this summer, with widespread availability of the cable access system to follow in the fall.
Cable TV networks are generally one-way systems, and one of the problems hampering the introduction of Internet access via cable has been figuring out how to make it a two-way information highway.
U.S. Robotics' system works by downloading information from the Internet at high speeds via cable but making requests for that information via a telephone line.
A two-way cable access system is expected to be available early next year, the company said. The system is for cable operators which have already converted to a two-way system.

"... Our approach is designed to eliminate the inhibitors to a mass market for cable modems and establish a true retail environment," U.S. Robotics Chairman Casey Cowell said in a statement. "This strategic approach dramatically reduces capital costs at every point in the network and makes cable Internet access a far more practical reality."
Competing cable modems are offered by, among others, Motorola Inc., Hewlett-Packard Co. and Zenith Electronics Inc.
Connecting to the Internet or online services via cable is more costly than via telephone lines and there is no standard for the technology.

A host of technical problems and a shortage of new capital among debt-laden cable TV service operators for investing in upgrading has slowed the introduction of cable modems to cable TV subscribers with computers.

Industry analysts have said a mass market must be developed for cable modems to be a success. Currently, most cable operators buy modems and provide them to subscribers much like set-top boxes. But U.S. Robotics said it is involved in establishing a cable modem standard and plans to stock its cable modems on retail shelves.
U.S. Robotics stock climbed $2.375 to $58.75 on Nasdaq.
